title: List
html:
A list is Python's dynamic array: an ordered, index-addressable, resizable collection (the same idea as C++ std::vector, Java ArrayList and the JavaScript Array). Arrays are the foundation that almost every other data structure is built on, so knowing exactly what is cheap and what is expensive on one is the first DSA skill.

Array — a block of elements stored in contiguous memory, so element i lives at base + i × size. That one formula is why reading arr[i] costs O(1) for any i.

Dynamic array (list) — an array that grows on demand. It keeps some spare capacity; when that runs out it allocates a bigger block, copies everything over and frees the old one. Python lists may also mix element types ([2, 'p', True]) because each slot stores a reference to an object, not the object itself.

How a dynamic array grows

The list pre-allocates a little extra room. append writes into that room in O(1). Only when the room is gone does the list resize:

1
Allocate a bigger block
Typically a multiple of the current capacity (×2 in most textbooks and in C++ vector; CPython uses a gentler ≈1.125× plus a constant, Java ArrayList uses 1.5×).
2
Copy
Move all n existing elements into the new block — this is the O(n) step.
3
Free the old block
The list now points at the new memory and has spare capacity again.
Why append is O(1) amortised

Append 1 000 numbers to an empty list that starts with room for 10. Resizes happen at 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640 elements — 7 copies totalling about 1 270 element moves, i.e. roughly one extra move per append. The occasional O(n) copy is spread over the O(n) cheap appends that follow it, so each append costs O(1) amortised.

With doubling, inserting n elements costs at most n + (1 + 2 + 4 + … + n) < 3n element writes → O(1) amortised per append

Random access

arr[i] is one multiplication and one memory read — O(1) for any index.

Cache friendly

Elements sit next to each other, so iterating pulls whole cache lines of useful data (locality of reference).

Slow in the middle

Inserting or deleting at index i shifts every element after it — O(n). Searching an unsorted array is also O(n).

Operations and their complexities

OperationPythonTimeWhy

Pitfall

l.insert(0, x) and l.pop(0) look innocent but shift the whole list every time — a loop of them is O(n²). Use collections.deque when you need cheap operations at the front.

Indexing and negative indices

Python lets you count from the back with negative indices; the other languages need n - k. Reading past either end is an IndexError in Python, an exception in Java, undefined in JavaScript and undefined behaviour in C++ (v.at(i) checks, v[i] does not).

Adding and searching

append goes to the end; insert makes room at an index by shifting. Membership (in), count and index all scan from the left — there is no faster way on an unsorted array.

Key point

Python's index() raises ValueError when the value is missing, while Java's indexOf and JavaScript's indexOf return -1. Check with in first, or catch the exception.

Removing elements

Three ways to remove in Python: remove(x) by value (first match), pop(i) by index returning the element, del l[i] / del l[a:b] by index or slice. Everything except popping from the end is O(n).

Pitfall

Never remove from a list while iterating over it with for x in l — elements shift under the loop and some get skipped. Build a new list ([x for x in l if keep(x)]) or iterate over a copy.

min, max, sum, reverse and sort

Two language-specific traps worth seeing once:

Slicing

l[start:stop:step] returns a new list with the elements from start up to but not including stop, every step-th one. Every part is optional; negative indices and a negative step work too. Slicing also works on tuples and strings.

SliceMeaningResult for [10, 20, 11, 40, 15, 19]
l[0:5]indices 0..4[10, 20, 11, 40, 15]
l[0:5:2]indices 0, 2, 4[10, 11, 15]
l[:]a shallow copy of everything[10, 20, 11, 40, 15, 19]
l[3:]from index 3 to the end[40, 15, 19]
l[:3]the first three[10, 20, 11]
l[-2:]the last two[15, 19]
l[::-1]reversed copy[19, 15, 40, 11, 20, 10]

A slice is a copy: equal in value (==) but a different object (is). Note that l in dup asks whether the whole list l is one of dup's elements — not whether the elements overlap.

Key point

t1 is t2 for two equal tuple literals is an implementation detail (CPython may or may not reuse the constant), so never rely on is for value comparison — use ==.

IdiomPythonC++JavaJavaScript

Pitfall

Java's subList(a, b) is a view of the original list, not a copy — changes to one show in the other. Wrap it in new ArrayList<>(…) when you need an independent copy.

Comprehensions

A comprehension builds a new collection from any iterable (a list, a range, a string, a file …) in one expression: [expression for item in iterable if condition]. It is the Pythonic replacement for the “make an empty list, loop, append” pattern — same O(n) time, less code.

The two list problems below, written as comprehensions:

Curly braces give a set or dict comprehension; zip pairs two lists up so dict(zip(keys, values)) builds a mapping.

The same filter → map idea exists everywhere; only Python has the dedicated syntax. Squares of the even numbers in 0..10:

Problem: average (mean) of a list

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 30, 40]
Output: 25.0
Input: l = [3, 4, 4]
Output: 3.7

Idea

Add everything up in one pass and divide by the count. The only things that go wrong are integer division (in C++ and Java 100 / 4 is 25 but 11 / 3 is 3) and an empty list (division by zero) — guard both.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Summing many large ints overflows in C++/Java — accumulate into a long long / long. Python integers never overflow, and never shadow the built-in sum with a variable called sum.

Problem: separate even and odd numbers

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 11, 40, 15, 19]
Output: even: 10 20 40 / odd: 11 15 19

Idea

One pass, one test per element: x % 2 == 0 sends it to the even list, everything else to the odd list. Order within each group is preserved.

Time O(n)Space O(n)
Key point

For negative numbers x % 2 is -1 in C++, Java and JavaScript but 1 in Python. Testing x % 2 == 0 (rather than == 1) is correct in every language.

Problem: elements smaller than x

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 11, 40, 15, 19], x = 21
Output: 10 20 11 15 19

Idea

A filter: keep each element that passes the test e < x. This is the shape of every “select the elements that …” problem — a single scan with a condition.

Time O(n)Space O(n)

Problem: largest element

Example

Input: l = [10, 5, 20, 8]
Output: 20
Input: l = []
Output: None

The naive approach checks, for every x, whether no element is bigger than it. Python's for … else runs the else only when the inner loop never hit break — handy, but the method is O(n²):

Idea

Keep a running maximum: start with the first element and replace it whenever you see something bigger. One pass, O(n). Return None for an empty list instead of crashing on l[0].

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

Initialising res = 0 instead of res = l[0] returns the wrong answer for an all-negative list such as [-3, -7].

Problem: second largest element

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 4, 5, 6, 1]
Output: 10
Input: l = [10, 10, 10]
Output: None

Two-pass version: find the largest, then the largest among elements not equal to it. Correct and O(n), but it reads the list twice:

Idea

Single pass with two trackers. When x beats the largest, the old largest becomes the second largest. When x is between them (and not equal to the largest), it becomes the new second. Duplicates of the maximum are ignored, so [10, 10, 10] has no second largest.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

sorted(l)[-2] is O(n log n) and wrong for [10, 10, 5] (gives 10). The one-pass version is the expected interview answer; mention explicitly how you treat duplicates.

Problem: check if a list is sorted

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 30]
Output: Yes
Input: l = [29, 24, 32]
Output: No

Naive: sort a copy and compare — O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space just to answer a yes/no question:

Idea

A list is sorted (non-decreasing) exactly when no adjacent pair is out of order. Scan once and return No the moment l[i] < l[i-1]. Equal neighbours are fine, and an empty or one-element list is trivially sorted.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Best case O(1) (the first pair is already out of order), worst case O(n). Ask the interviewer whether “sorted” means strictly increasing — then the test becomes l[i] <= l[i-1].

Problem: reverse a list

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 30, 40]
Output: 40 30 20 10

Python has four ready-made ways; reverse() works in place, the other three produce a new list:

Idea

The hand-written version worth remembering swaps the two ends and walks inward: l[s] ↔ l[e], s += 1, e -= 1, until the pointers meet. Only n / 2 swaps and no extra list — that is the “two-pointer” pattern used all over DSA.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
PythonC++JavaJavaScript
In placel.reverse()reverse(v.begin(), v.end())Collections.reverse(list)arr.reverse()
New reversed copyl[::-1], list(reversed(l))vector<int>(v.rbegin(), v.rend())copy, then reversearr.toReversed(), [...arr].reverse()

Problem: remove duplicates from a sorted array

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 20, 30, 30, 30, 30]
Output: 10 20 30, size = 3

Because the array is sorted, all copies of a value sit next to each other, so a duplicate is simply an element equal to the one just before it. The naive version writes the distinct values into a second array — correct, but O(n) extra space:

Idea

Do it in place with two pointers: res marks where the next distinct value should be written, i scans. Whenever arr[i] differs from the last written value arr[res-1], copy it to arr[res] and advance res. The first res slots hold the answer; what remains after them is garbage.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Pitfall

The two-pointer trick requires sorted input. On an unsorted array ([10, 20, 20, 30, 40, 30, 30]) you must either sort first (O(n log n)) or use a set (O(n) extra space) — equal values are no longer adjacent. The original notes sorted inside the function; do that only when the problem does not promise sorted input.

Problem: left rotate by one

Example

Input: l = [10, 20, 30, 40]
Output: 20 30 40 10

A left (counter-clockwise) rotation moves the first element to the end and every other element one step to the left. Python can do it with slicing or pop/append:

Idea

By hand: save l[0], shift every element one place left (l[i-1] = l[i]), then put the saved value in the last slot. One pass, no extra array.

Time O(n)Space O(1)
Key point

Rotating by d positions by repeating this d times costs O(n·d). The O(n) answer is the reversal algorithm: reverse the first d, reverse the rest, then reverse the whole array — covered in DSA Advanced → Arrays.

Collecting input into a list: chicken or duck

A small competitive-programming exercise from the notes that shows the standard pattern of reading T test cases into a list first and processing them afterwards. A chicken has X legs, a duck Y legs; given Z legs in total, could they all be chickens (Z % X == 0), all ducks, either (Any) or neither (Null)?

Example

Input: 4 cases: (2 3 6), (2 3 4), (2 3 9), (2 3 7)
Output: Any / Chicken / Duck / Null

Time O(T)Space O(T)
Key point

Reading all of standard input in one go (sys.stdin.read(), readFileSync(0)) is much faster than calling input() in a loop when there are thousands of lines — a common cause of “Time Limit Exceeded”.

Interview Q&A

Why is appending to a dynamic array O(1) amortised and not O(1) worst case?

A single append can trigger a resize that copies all n elements — that one call is O(n). But after growing by a constant factor the next ~n appends are free, so the total cost of n appends is O(n) and the average per append is O(1). Worst case for one call remains O(n); amortised analysis spreads the rare expensive call over the cheap ones.

Array vs linked list — when would you pick each?

Arrays: O(1) random access, cache-friendly, less memory per element; but O(n) insert/delete in the middle. Linked lists: O(1) insert/delete at a known node and no resizing; but O(n) to reach the k-th element and poor locality. For most workloads arrays (vectors) win; linked lists shine for queues/deques and when you hold references to nodes.

What is the difference between l.sort() and sorted(l)? Between l.reverse() and l[::-1]?

l.sort() and l.reverse() modify the list in place and return None; sorted(l) and l[::-1] leave l alone and return a new list. A classic bug is l = l.sort(), which sets l to None.

Why does [[0] * 3] * 3 behave strangely?

The outer * copies the reference to the same inner list three times, so changing grid[0][0] changes every row. Build nested lists with a comprehension: [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)].

How do you find the second largest in one pass, and what about duplicates?

Track largest and second. If x > largest, demote largest to second and take x; else if x != largest and x > second, update second. Skipping x == largest means duplicates of the maximum do not count — [10, 10, 5] gives 5, and [10, 10] gives None. State that convention aloud.

Removing duplicates: why does the in-place solution need sorted input?

It only compares each element with the last kept one, which is enough when equal values are adjacent. For unsorted input equal values can be far apart, so you need a hash set (O(n) space) or a sort first (O(n log n)).
